`animate*AsState` hides its value behind a declarative API that can only ever animate towards a new target, so an instant reset needs `Animatable`, which hands you the value and imperative control over it.

### The three tools
- **`animate*AsState`** — fire and forget. It wraps an `Animatable` you cannot reach: you set a target, it retargets whatever is in flight, and there is no `snapTo`, no `stop`, and no way to ask whether it is running beyond a `finishedListener`. You can pass `animationSpec = snap()` for the frames where you want no motion, but choosing the spec from state to work around the API is a sign you picked the wrong one.
- **`Animatable`** — you own it in a `remember` and drive it from a coroutine: `snapTo(v)` sets the value with no animation, `animateTo(v, spec, initialVelocity)` animates, `stop()` halts it, `updateBounds` clamps it. Underneath it is a `MutatorMutex`, so a second `animateTo` cancels the first cleanly rather than two animations fighting over one value.
- **`updateTransition(state)`** — one state change driving several values (`animateDp`, `animateColor`, `animateFloat`) off a shared clock, so they cannot drift apart and they all retarget together when the state flips mid-flight.

### Interruption is the dividing line
None of them restart from zero when the target changes: a `spring` carries the current velocity into the retarget, which is why rapid toggling feels continuous. What `animate*AsState` cannot survive is interruption by anything that is *not* a new target — a finger grabbing the value, a reset, a fling.

State to one value, `animate*AsState`. One state to many values, `updateTransition`. Anything a gesture or an event must seize control of, `Animatable`.

The content lambda ignores its own parameter and reads the captured `count`, so the outgoing content recomposes to the new number as well and you are cross-fading a value with an identical copy of itself.

### Read the lambda parameter
- `AnimatedContent` keeps the leaving and the arriving content composed at the same time while the transition runs. The lambda receives the state that piece of content was composed for: `{ target -> Text("Total: $target") }`.
- Reading the captured value makes the leaving copy show the arriving number. The animation runs perfectly — it is simply invisible.
- `contentKey = { it.id }` declares which state changes count as *the same* content, so an unrelated field changing does not trigger a swap.

### Enter, exit and size
- `transitionSpec = { fadeIn() togetherWith fadeOut() }` builds a `ContentTransform` from the enter of the arriving content and the exit of the leaving one. `togetherWith` replaced the old `with` infix.
- A `SizeTransform` is attached by default, so the container animates between the two sizes and clips while it does — that is why a counter growing from "9" to "10" widens smoothly. `.using(SizeTransform(clip = false))` turns the clipping off; `null` makes the box jump.

### AnimatedVisibility
`AnimatedVisibility(visible, enter = fadeIn() + expandVertically(), exit = fadeOut())` keeps its children in the composition until the exit finishes — that delay is the entire point, and it is why you never wrap it in an `if`. Children stagger with `Modifier.animateEnterExit`, and a `MutableTransitionState` seeded `false` then set to `true` runs the enter animation on first composition, which a plain `Boolean` cannot.

`Modifier.animateItem()` on the item's root animates placement, appearance and disappearance — but only for items with stable `key`s, because without one an item is identified by its index and a reorder is indistinguishable from a content change.

### What the modifier covers
- `Modifier.animateItem(fadeInSpec, placementSpec, fadeOutSpec)` lives in `LazyItemScope` and replaces the deprecated `Modifier.animateItemPlacement()`, which only handled moves. Passing `null` for any of the three switches that part off.
- It animates *position and presence*. An item whose own content grows still needs `Modifier.animateContentSize()` or an `AnimatedVisibility` inside it.
- Removal animation only runs if the item actually leaves the list; filtering the source before it reaches `items` is why "my delete does not fade" usually turns out to be a data problem.

### Keys are the mechanism
- `items(list, key = { it.id })`. With no `key`, the list keys by index: the item at index 3 stays the item at index 3 and there is nothing to move.
- The key must be stable across reloads and unique. `key = { it.hashCode() }` on a data class whose fields change hands out a new key for the same row, which reads as a removal plus an insertion — the row fades out and back in on every edit.
- It must also be saveable (String, Int, Parcelable): the key is what restores scroll position and per-item `rememberSaveable` state.
- Add `contentType = { it.kind }` in a mixed list so Compose reuses a matching slot instead of throwing the composition away.

### The trap
The modifier has to be on the item's own outermost modifier. Put it on a `Text` two levels down and nothing animates, because the node that moves is the item root, not that child.

Both composables must sit under one `SharedTransitionLayout`, carry `Modifier.sharedElement` with the *same* key, and each be inside an `AnimatedVisibilityScope` — the transition is what tells the layout when those two nodes are one thing in flight.

### The four pieces
1. `SharedTransitionLayout { }` wraps both destinations, so it goes *outside* the `NavHost`, never inside one screen. It provides `SharedTransitionScope`.
2. `Modifier.sharedElement(rememberSharedContentState(key = "cover-$id"), animatedVisibilityScope = …)` on the row image and on the detail image. The keys must match exactly and be unique among visible content.
3. The `AnimatedVisibilityScope` comes from whatever animates the swap: an `AnimatedContent`, an `AnimatedVisibility`, or the `composable { }` lambda of a `NavHost`, whose receiver is an `AnimatedContentScope`. No transition, no shared element.
4. `Modifier.sharedBounds(...)` instead when the two are not the same content — a title that changes size, a card that becomes a screen — with `resizeMode = ScaleToBounds()` or `RemeasureToBounds`.

### Where it draws
While the transition runs the element is lifted into the layout's overlay and drawn above everything, which is how it escapes parents that would clip it. It is also the surprise: it draws over your app bar. `zIndexInOverlay`, `clipInOverlayDuringTransition` and `renderInSharedTransitionScopeOverlay` on the other content are the levers.

### Where it breaks
- Two visible elements sharing a key, or a key built from an index instead of an id.
- The screen composed outside the `NavHost` scope, so there is no `AnimatedVisibilityScope` to hand down.
- Text reflowing mid-flight; `Modifier.skipToLookaheadSize()` lays it out at its final size while the bounds animate.
- It is still an opt-in API (`@ExperimentalSharedTransitionApi`) — pin the opt-in in one place rather than sprinkling it.

Take the spring unless the exact curve is the point, because a spring carries the current velocity into a retarget while a `tween` restarts its curve from wherever the value happened to be and visibly stutters.

### The specs
- `spring(dampingRatio, stiffness, visibilityThreshold)` — physics, no duration. Interrupt it and it continues from the current value *and velocity*, which is what makes gesture-driven and rapidly-toggled motion feel continuous. It is the default for `animate*AsState` and `Animatable` for exactly that reason.
- `tween(durationMillis, delayMillis, easing)` — a fixed duration and curve: `FastOutSlowInEasing`, `LinearOutSlowInEasing`, or a `CubicBezierEasing(a, b, c, d)` copied straight out of the design tool. Right when a curve was specified, when something must finish in step with something else, and for colour and alpha, where physics buys nothing.
- `keyframes { durationMillis = 375; 0.9f at 0 using LinearOutSlowInEasing; 1.08f at 250 }` for multi-stage motion — an overshoot, a wobble. `keyframesWithSpline` interpolates multi-dimensional values such as `Offset` along a smooth path instead of segment by segment. `snap`, `repeatable` and `infiniteRepeatable` round the set out.

### What visibilityThreshold protects
A spring approaches its target asymptotically and never mathematically arrives, so it needs a "close enough" value at which it snaps to the target and reports itself finished. Every built-in `animate*AsState` passes the right one for its type — `Dp.VisibilityThreshold` is `0.1.dp`, `IntOffset`'s is one pixel — but a bare `Animatable(0f)` gets the generic `0.01f`. Animate raw pixels with that and the spring keeps producing frames long after the movement is invisible: a wasted frame per tick, forever, on a value nobody can see move.

Material 3 ships a `MotionScheme` (`MaterialTheme.motionScheme.fastSpatialSpec()`), which is the honest way to give a designer a vocabulary that is not a duration.

During the drag you `snapTo` each new value so nothing animates, and on release you feed the tracked velocity into `animateDecay` — or into `animateTo(target, initialVelocity = v)` — so the motion continues from the speed the finger left behind.

### The loop
1. On `awaitFirstDown`, call `offset.stop()`. A fling from the previous gesture may still be running and would fight the finger for the same value.
2. For each drag change, `launch { offset.snapTo(offset.value + delta) }` and `change.consume()`. `snapTo` is a suspend function that sets the value with no animation and cancels whatever was running, because `Animatable` serialises everything through a `MutatorMutex`.
3. Feed a `VelocityTracker` with `addPosition(change.uptimeMillis, change.position)` and read `calculateVelocity()` on release. `Modifier.draggable` hands you that velocity in `onDragStopped` for free; the raw `pointerInput` loop does not.
4. `val decay = splineBasedDecay<Float>(this)` is density-aware and matches platform flings. `decay.calculateTargetValue(current, velocity)` tells you where the fling *would* land before you start it, which is how you decide between coasting and springing back.
5. `offset.animateDecay(velocity, decay)` to coast, or `offset.animateTo(0f, spring(), initialVelocity = velocity)` to return without throwing away the throw.

### Traps
- Keeping the value in a `mutableStateOf` and moving it by hand from a `LaunchedEffect` loses velocity, interruption and bounds. `Animatable` exists for exactly this.
- `snapTo` is `suspend`, so it cannot be called from a plain drag callback — `launch` it and let the mutex order the writes.
- `offset.updateBounds(lower, upper)` clamps the decay so a hard fling stops at the edge instead of leaving the screen.
- Read the value in `Modifier.offset { IntOffset(...) }`, the lambda overload: it defers the read to layout, so a frame costs a re-layout instead of recomposing the subtree.

The `pointerInput` block is a coroutine launched once and cancelled and restarted only when its keys change, so with `Unit` as the key it captured the first `onSelect` and holds that instance for the node's whole life.

### How the block runs
- `Modifier.pointerInput(key1) { ... }` starts a suspending `PointerInputScope` coroutine. Changing a key cancels the running block — mid-gesture, if a gesture is in flight — and launches a fresh one. `Unit` means "never restart".
- Inside, `awaitPointerEventScope { }` is where events are actually awaited: `awaitFirstDown()`, `awaitPointerEvent(pass)`, `drag(pointerId) { }`, `awaitTouchSlopOrCancellation(id) { change, over -> }`. The `detectTapGestures` and `detectDragGestures` helpers are thin wrappers over exactly this.

### Two fixes and their cost
- `val select by rememberUpdatedState(onSelect)`, then call `select` inside the block. The coroutine keeps running, gestures in flight survive, and the read always sees the latest lambda. This is the default answer.
- `Modifier.pointerInput(onSelect) { }` also works, but it restarts the coroutine whenever the lambda's identity changes — and an unmemoised lambda changes on every recomposition, so you cancel the gesture the user is in the middle of. Key on something stable, such as `item.id`, if you key at all.

### Consumption and passes
`change.consume()` marks a change as handled. Parents and siblings still receive the event, but the built-in detectors skip consumed changes, and that is how a child wins a contested gesture. Events travel `Initial` (parent first) → `Main` (child first, the default) → `Final` (back up), so a parent that must steal a drag listens on `Initial` and consumes there. Modifier order matters too: `Modifier.padding(8.dp).pointerInput { }` leaves the padding untouchable, the reverse order includes it.

No ripple, nothing for TalkBack to activate, and no keyboard or D-pad focus — `clickable` is not a tap listener, it is a tap listener plus indication, semantics and focus, and `detectTapGestures` is only the listener.

### What clickable adds
- **Indication.** It feeds an `InteractionSource` and draws `LocalIndication.current`, which under a Material theme is `ripple()`. Press, hover and focus visuals all come off that one source.
- **Semantics.** It publishes an `onClick` action plus `role` and `onClickLabel`, so TalkBack announces "Button, double-tap to activate" and can actually fire it. Accessibility services never synthesise touch events — they invoke the semantics action, and a bare `pointerInput` node has none.
- **Focus and keys.** The node becomes focusable, and Enter, Space and a D-pad centre press call `onClick`. That is your entire keyboard, TV and Chromebook story.
- Plus `enabled = false` handling and hover feedback on desktop and web.

### What to use instead
`Modifier.combinedClickable(onClick =, onLongClick =, onDoubleClick =)` gives you the extra gestures and keeps all of the above. Drop to `detectTapGestures` only for something that genuinely is not a click — a tap on a canvas, a press-and-hold on a crop handle — and then add `Modifier.semantics { onClick(label) { … } }` and `Modifier.indication(...)` back by hand.

### The 48dp target
`clickable` does *not* enforce a minimum touch target. Material components get one from `minimumInteractiveComponentSize()`; for your own 24dp icon, put the padding *inside* the clickable — `Modifier.clickable { }.padding(12.dp).size(24.dp)` — so the node measures 48dp. And clip before you make it clickable, or the ripple paints a rectangle over your rounded card.

`AnchoredDraggableState` has nowhere to settle until it is given anchors, and until `updateAnchors` has run its offset is `Float.NaN` — both symptoms are the same missing step.

### The four pieces
- The state owns the current value and the offset in pixels; `DraggableAnchors { Settled at 0f; Dismissed at -width }` is the map from a value to a position.
- Anchors are a measurement result, so they can only be built once the row has a width: `state.updateAnchors(...)` from `Modifier.onSizeChanged`, or `Modifier.draggableAnchors(state, Orientation.Horizontal) { size, _ -> anchors to newTarget }`.
- `Modifier.anchoredDraggable(state, Orientation.Horizontal)` only reads the gesture. Nothing moves until you apply the offset yourself, normally with `Modifier.offset { IntOffset(state.requireOffset().roundToInt(), 0) }`.
- Settling is decided by two thresholds: `positionalThreshold`, which is handed the distance between anchors and returns the pixel past which the drag commits, and `velocityThreshold`, above which a short flick commits anyway.

### What catches people
- Reading `state.offset` up in composition recomposes the row on every frame of the drag; read it inside the `offset { }` lambda so only placement re-runs.
- `currentValue` flips as soon as a target is chosen, `settledValue` only when the animation lands — remove the item on `settledValue`, and veto impossible transitions in `confirmValueChange`.
- Newer Foundation releases move the settle rules into a `FlingBehavior` built with `AnchoredDraggableDefaults` instead of the state constructor; same concepts, different place to pass them.
- `swipeable` and `rememberSwipeableState` are the deprecated ancestors of all this, and Material 3's `SwipeToDismissBox` is what you should use when you do not need custom anchors.

Treat anchors as output of layout, never as constants.

The header is consuming the downward delta in `onPreScroll`, where it gets first refusal; expanding belongs in `onPostScroll`, on what the list did not use.

### How a nested scroll travels
- Every delta goes outwards-in and then back out: `onPreScroll` runs from the outermost connection down to the scrolling child, the child consumes what it wants, then `onPostScroll` runs from the child back up. Flings mirror this with `onPreFling` and `onPostFling`, both of which are `suspend` and receive a `Velocity`.
- Each callback returns the `Offset` it consumed. `Offset.Zero` passes everything through; claiming more than was available shows up as a scroll that sticks.
- `source` says where the delta came from — `NestedScrollSource.UserInput` for a finger, `SideEffect` for a fling or an animation, `Wheel` for a mouse. Foundation 1.7 renamed `Drag` and `Fling` to those first two.

### The two directions
1. Finger moving up, `available.y < 0`: consume in `onPreScroll` while the header still has room to shrink. The header must give way before the list moves at all.
2. Finger moving down, `available.y > 0`: consume nothing in pre-scroll, and take what is left in `onPostScroll` — which is zero until the list has actually reached its top.

Keep the offset in a `mutableFloatStateOf` and let the header read it inside `graphicsLayer { }`, so a scroll frame costs a redraw rather than a recomposition of the header's content.

Material 3 already ships this shape: `TopAppBarDefaults.enterAlwaysScrollBehavior(rememberTopAppBarState())` plus `Modifier.nestedScroll(scrollBehavior.nestedScrollConnection)`, with pinned and exit-until-collapsed variants alongside it. Write the connection yourself only when the motion is not one of those.

Pre-scroll is where a parent takes priority; post-scroll is where it takes leftovers.

There is no arena and no negotiation: the first node to call `consume()` on a pointer change owns the gesture, and the order is fixed by the three passes every event makes through the modifier chain.

### The three passes
- Each `PointerEvent` is delivered to every node three times — `Initial` from the outermost node inwards, `Main` from the innermost node outwards, then `Final` inwards again.
- Ordinary detectors work on `Main`, so the innermost node gets first claim. After `change.consume()`, everything further out sees `change.isConsumed` and stands down.
- `Initial` is how a parent takes an event before its children see it, which is how a modal scrim swallows taps. `Final` is how a node learns that somebody else took the gesture and cancels its own highlight.

### Why the drag ate the scroll
- `detectDragGestures` is direction-agnostic: it waits for touch slop in any direction and consumes as soon as slop is crossed, so a mostly-vertical finger is claimed by the row before the list's `scrollable` ever sees it.
- Orientation-locked detectors are the fix. `detectHorizontalDragGestures` and `awaitHorizontalTouchSlopOrCancellation` only claim horizontal movement — which is exactly why a `HorizontalPager` inside a `verticalScroll` needs no special handling at all.
- Better still, `Modifier.draggable(orientation = Orientation.Horizontal)`: it is orientation-aware and participates in nested scroll instead of competing with it.
- Two scrollables on the same axis never fight over pointers. The inner one scrolls and hands its leftovers outwards through nested scroll.

Pick the narrowest detector that describes your gesture, and remember that consuming is a claim you cannot take back.

Alpha is being applied to each drawing command separately instead of to the composited group, and `compositingStrategy` is what selects between those two behaviours.

### What a graphics layer is
- `Modifier.graphicsLayer { }` puts the subtree into its own render node carrying `translationX/Y`, `scaleX/Y`, `rotationZ`, `alpha`, `shadowElevation`, `shape`, `clip`, `transformOrigin` and `renderEffect`. Changing any of them re-draws the layer with new properties; nothing is measured again.
- `CompositingStrategy.ModulateAlpha` multiplies alpha into every draw instruction. It is cheap and allocates no buffer, and overlapping children show through each other exactly as you are seeing.
- `CompositingStrategy.Offscreen` renders the subtree into an offscreen buffer and composites it once, so the group fades as a single object. It also clips to the layer bounds, and it is what a `BlendMode` needs in order to see the pixels underneath.
- `Auto` is the default and leaves the decision to the runtime; a `renderEffect` or a non-opaque alpha is what pushes it towards an offscreen buffer.

### Why the lambda form matters
- `Modifier.graphicsLayer { translationY = scroll }` reads `scroll` in the draw phase, so a change invalidates drawing only — a 60 fps parallax costs no recomposition and no layout.
- The parameter form, `Modifier.graphicsLayer(translationY = scroll)`, reads the value in composition, so every frame recomposes the caller. Same distinction as `Modifier.offset { }` against `Modifier.offset(x.dp)`, one phase later.
- `alpha = 0f` still measures, places and draws the subtree. To make something genuinely go away, stop composing it.

The lambda for anything that changes per frame; the parameter form only for something that changes when a user taps.

`drawWithCache` splits the modifier in two: the outer block re-runs only when the size changes or a state it read changes, and the `onDraw*` block it returns runs every frame — so the `Path` and the `Brush` are built once and reused.

### The four ways to draw
- `Modifier.drawBehind { }` gives you a `DrawScope` behind the content and is executed on every draw pass; anything allocated inside is allocated per frame.
- `Modifier.drawWithContent { drawContent(); ... }` lets you decide where the children land in the drawing order, which is how you paint a scrim, a badge or a `BlendMode` mask over them.
- `Modifier.drawWithCache { val path = ...; onDrawBehind { } }` is the caching version of both — `onDrawWithContent` is its content-aware sibling.
- `Canvas(modifier) { }` is literally `Spacer(modifier.drawBehind(onDraw))`: a leaf with no children and no intrinsic size, so it draws nothing until a size modifier gives it one.

### Getting the caching right
- Read the animated value inside `onDrawBehind`, never in the cache block. A state read in the cache block invalidates the cache every frame and you are back where you started.
- Drawing is the last phase, so a draw modifier that reads an animated state invalidates drawing alone — no recomposition, no layout. That is why a progress ring belongs in a draw modifier rather than in a stack of animated `Box` sizes.
- `DrawScope` works in pixels and is itself a `Density`, so `12.dp.toPx()` is available inside it.
- Text needs `rememberTextMeasurer()` and `drawText`; measuring text per frame is the other classic allocation in `drawBehind`. `drawIntoCanvas { it.nativeCanvas }` is the escape hatch to a platform API Compose does not expose.

Build in the cache block, paint in the draw block.

`Modifier.blur` is real only from Android 12 (API 31) and `RuntimeShader` with AGSL only from Android 13 (API 33), so both have to degrade to something you drew yourself.

### What the platform gives you
- `Modifier.blur(radius, edgeTreatment)` is backed by `RenderEffect` and needs API 31. Below that it is a silent no-op — the content renders sharp rather than broken, which is exactly why it survives review on a modern test device.
- The same thing at layer level, and animatable: `graphicsLayer { renderEffect = BlurEffect(radiusX, radiusY, TileMode.Decal) }`.
- `RuntimeShader` compiles an AGSL program at API 33+. Use it as a fill with `ShaderBrush(shader)`, or run the composable's own pixels through it with `RenderEffect.createRuntimeShaderEffect(shader, "content").asComposeRenderEffect()`.
- Blurring what is behind your *window* is a different feature: `Window.setBackgroundBlurRadius` on API 31+, which the system may disable outright — check `WindowManager.isCrossWindowBlurEnabled()` before designing around it.

### The fallback you owe
- Gate on `Build.VERSION.SDK_INT` once, in the composable that owns the panel, and choose the whole look there: a blur above 31, a translucent scrim over a `Brush.verticalGradient` below it. Do not scatter version checks through the tree.
- Gradients cost nothing anywhere: `Brush.linearGradient`, `radialGradient` and `sweepGradient` work on every supported release, and a `Brush` also fills text through `TextStyle(brush = ...)`.
- Blur costs GPU time proportional to radius and area, and animating the radius re-runs the effect at a new size every frame. Animate the alpha of a fixed-radius blur instead.

Treat blur and shaders as a progressive enhancement on top of a design that already works with a gradient.

Wrap the changing region in a `LookaheadScope`: it measures and places the subtree twice per frame — once for where everything is going, once for where you actually draw it — so each node can animate from its current bounds towards a target it can see.

### Why the obvious tools cannot do it
- `Modifier.animateContentSize` animates one node's own size and nothing about its position, and it cannot follow a child that ended up under a different parent.
- `animate*AsState` into an `offset` needs the destination in pixels, and in a real layout only the parent knows that, and only after measuring.
- Intrinsics answer "how big would you like to be" during an ordinary pass. That is a static question; it never tells you where a node is heading.
- `SubcomposeLayout` composes children during layout, so discovering a target with it means composing the subtree twice a frame and opting out of the cheap single-pass path. Lookahead gets the same information without composing anything twice.

### The mechanism
1. `LookaheadScope { }` around the region. The lookahead pass computes each child's target size and position as if the change had already finished.
2. `Modifier.approachLayout(isMeasurementApproachInProgress, approachMeasure)` — stable since Foundation 1.7, replacing the experimental `intermediateLayout` — measures with your own animated constraints while the animation runs, and reports when it is done so Compose returns to the fast path.
3. `Modifier.animateBounds(lookaheadScope)` in `androidx.compose.animation` is the ready-made version of size and position together. `SharedTransitionLayout` is the same machinery with matched keys.

Two traps: an `isMeasurementApproachInProgress` that never returns false pins the subtree in the approach pass forever, and a node outside the scope has no target to animate towards — the scope boundary is the animation's boundary.

Compose reads the system animator duration scale through a `MotionDurationScale` element in the recomposer's coroutine context, so animations started from the composition jump straight to their target at scale 0 — one started on a scope you built yourself carries no such element and ignores the setting entirely.

### How the setting reaches an animation
- "Remove animations" in Accessibility and the animator scale in developer options both write `Settings.Global.ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE`. Zero means do not animate; 10x means ten times longer.
- The recomposer that drives your window installs a `MotionDurationScale` reading that value. Every `animate*AsState`, `Transition`, `AnimatedVisibility` and `Animatable.animateTo` launched from the composition inherits it through the coroutine context.
- `LaunchedEffect` and `rememberCoroutineScope()` are composition scopes and inherit it. `viewModelScope`, a `CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Main)` you constructed, or a callback from a plain listener do not — that is where the slide-in came from.

### What you still owe the user
- A loop has no end to jump to: a `rememberInfiniteTransition` shimmer, a pulsing dot, an auto-advancing carousel. Check the flag yourself and render the still frame.
- On API 26+ that check is `ValueAnimator.areAnimatorsEnabled()`; below it, read `ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE` from `Settings.Global` directly.
- Large translate-and-scale motion, parallax and autoplay are a vestibular problem rather than a matter of taste, so gate them on the same flag and keep the flag in one `CompositionLocal` instead of branching per screen.
- Tests see none of this — the Compose clock is virtual. Drive motion by hand with `composeTestRule.mainClock.autoAdvance = false` plus `advanceTimeBy(...)` so an assertion lands mid-flight; leave autoAdvance on and `waitForIdle` never returns on an infinite animation.

If a coroutine you created starts the animation, honouring the setting is your job.
